title: The surah without bismillah
hookLine: the only surah that doesn't open with bismillah, which scholars link to its opening in 9:1

lines: BISMILLAH, A HUNDRED AND THIRTEEN TIMES.
cards: Way back at the start of this path, you learned bismillah: in the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Since then you've seen it stand at the top of surah after surah, a hundred and thirteen times, a doorway you walk through without looking. Open a printed Qur'an to surah nine, and the doorway isn't there.
The page goes straight from the last line of surah eight to the first line of surah nine, and reciters who begin there don't say it. Out of a hundred and fourteen surahs, it's the only one.
People have been asking why for fourteen centuries.

teach.b: Surah nine has two names. At-Tawbah, Repentance, for the repentance it describes later on. And Bara'ah, from its first word: a release, a disavowal, a declared end to obligations.
In Pickthall's words, it opens: “Freedom from obligation (is proclaimed) from Allah and His messenger toward those of the idolaters with whom ye made a treaty.”
It's a proclamation about treaties that had been broken, read out at the pilgrimage in the ninth year after the emigration.
The verses that follow make an exception: those who kept their treaties are to be honored to the end of their term. Why no bismillah?
Scholars give two main explanations. One comes from a report in which the young scholar Ibn Abbas asked the caliph Uthman this very question.

Uthman answered that surah eight was among the early Medinan revelations and surah nine among the last, that their content was similar, and that the Prophet ﷺ died without making clear whether nine was part of eight.
So the compilers set them side by side and left out the line between them.
The second explanation is attributed to Ali: the bismillah is a promise of safety, and this surah opens with that safety withdrawn from treaty-breakers. Many scholars hold both together.
One more detail: the bismillah still appears a hundred and fourteen times in the Qur'an. Surah twenty-seven contains it inside a verse, in a letter from the prophet Sulayman. The count stays whole.
Only this doorway is silent, and the silence itself became something to study.

how: When reciting surah nine from its beginning, Muslims do not say the bismillah; many begin with a'udhu billah instead, and in printed copies of the Qur'an the surah follows surah eight with no basmala line.

o: a release, a declared end to obligations
a promise of safety from God
repentance, a turning back to God

games.q: inside the surah's opening — tap the pairs.
p: unclear if nine was part of eight

s: surah nine is the only surah without an opening bismillah
one of a hundred and fourteen, and the only one.
because of this, the bismillah appears only 113 times in the Qur'an
surah twenty-seven contains it in Sulayman's letter, so the count is still 114.
the opening proclamation covered every treaty, kept or broken
the verses that follow exempt those who kept their treaties, to the end of their term.

games.q: you're Ibn Abbas, and you ask Uthman why surahs eight and nine sit together with no bismillah between them. what does he say?
o: the Prophet died without making clear whether nine was part of eight.
it was too long to fit.
games.why: their content was similar and the Prophet hadn't made clear whether they were one, so the compilers left out the line (Tirmidhi; Abu Dawud).

practice: Notice a place in your day where words are usually said, and listen for the gap instead: a greeting that wasn't given, a thank-you skipped, a bismillah forgotten before eating.
Don't fix it yet; just notice that a missing word can say as much as a spoken one.

wordCard.voice: Bara'ah, a release, a disavowal. At-Tawbah's other name, the first word of surah nine, the one surah that opens without in the name of God. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a release, a disavowal; the first word of surah nine and one of its names.

carryVoice: Your line: the silence speaks. Even a gap on the page can teach. That's day four hundred twenty-one.
